text: Project documentsArchitecture Code

Overview
The project compares outcomes after simultaneous liver–kidney (SLK) transplantation in recipients with and without HIV, using SRTR standard analysis files loaded through the separate sRtr package. It works in five stages:

Load the liver and kidney transplant files and pair each person’s liver and kidney records.
Keep first SLK transplants, apply exclusions, classify HIV status, and derive analysis variables.
Add donor and candidate variables.
Prepare data for propensity score matching (the matching itself runs outside the repository; see Matching).
Fit Cox and length-of-stay models in the matched cohort and produce tables and figures.

A Quarto website in quarto/ is rendered by .github/workflows/publish.yml and published to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves; the local render in docs/ is not committed. Its pages were adapted from another project and do not yet describe this project’s scripts.

Script and Object Flow
R/main.R sources scripts in order, and scripts share objects through the global environment. The diagram shows what main.R sources (solid) and what later steps need but main.R does not source (dashed).












Current state of the pipeline
main.R does not run end to end at this commit:

R/functions/functions.R defines helpers, then builds results tables from model objects (cox_main, cox_kidney, cox_liver and others) and fits interaction models from matched_df. Those objects do not exist when main.R sources the file second, so the run stops there.
R/modeling/modeling.R and R/tables/tables.R do not parse: each contains R Markdown text and chunk fences. main.R does not source modeling.R.
R/matching/matching.R saves the matching data and stops; the code that reads the matched result back and builds matched_df is inside if (FALSE).
R/tables/tables.R needs matched_df, the fitted models, and label_list from matched_tables.R, none of which main.R creates.
main.R sources R/figures.R, which does not exist; the figures script is R/figures/figures.R.

Components

Setup
Purpose: Load libraries and define table labels.
Location: R/setup.R
Key symbols: - Libraries for data management, sRtr, strobe and flowchart, MatchIt, survival, MASS, sandwich, lmtest, gtsummary, gt, survminer - conflict_prefer() calls so dplyr::select, filter and lag win - var_labels — named vector of readable labels for table variables
Analysis constants (study start year, age threshold, era cut-off, matching settings) are not defined here; they are hard-coded in the scripts that use them.


Helper functions
Location: R/functions/functions.R
Key functions: - combine_li_ki_consistent() — harmonizes a field recorded in both the liver and kidney files: positive if one is positive and the other positive or missing, negative likewise, missing when they conflict - recode_sex_FM(), recode_YNU(), recode_PNU(), recode_YNU_to_words(), collapse_donor_race(), make_missing_level() — recoders - make_gtsummary_labels() — converts var_labels for gtsummary - mk_tbl(), clean_labels() — gtsummary regression tables - extract_hiv_row(), extract_interaction(), extract_robust(), format_cox(), fit_cox_capture_warning() — model result extraction and formatting
The file also contains analysis code (results-table construction, a gtsave() to the project root, interaction models, and library() calls); see Current state.


Cohort construction
Location: R/primary_data_preparation/


















Script
What it does




import.R
Loads tx_li, tx_ki, donor_deceased, txf_li, txf_ki, malig, immuno, cand_kipa, cand_liin and pra_hist with load_srtr_file(); checks transplant dates are Date and DONOR_ID is present; full-joins liver and kidney records by PERS_ID (suffixes _LI, _KI); keeps pairs transplanted within one day of each other as tx_slkRaw


excluding_prior_transplants.R
Excludes prior transplants by the CAN_PREV_TX flags and by earlier transplant dates (first_tx); keeps each person’s first SLK; removes same-day duplicate records by a rule applied to graft failure dates; writes the duplicate records to data-private/ for manual review; stops unless one row per PERS_ID remains


combining_liver_kidney_variables.R
Creates harmonized hypertension, CMV, HCV, HBV core antibody, HBV surface antigen and malignancy variables with combine_li_ki_consistent()


create_hiv_data_set.R
Cleans REC_HIV_STAT in both files, excludes records positive in one file and negative in the other, and sets HIV_POSITIVE (positive in one file and positive or missing in the other); creates tx_slk_final


process_slk_data.R
Excludes different liver and kidney donors, recipients under 16, and kidney–liver–heart or –intestine transplants; derives donor BMI, graft failure and death times, composite transplant and death dates, recipient and donor characteristics, OPTN diagnosis groups, YEAR_TRANSPLANT, ERA (pre-DAA before 2014), MELD/PELD, causes of graft failure, payer, collapsed race and length of stay


create_liver_only_dataset.R
Starts a liver-only comparison cohort; writes records to data-private/ for manual review; the rest is inside if (FALSE)



Output: tx_slk_final, one row per SLK recipient with _LI and _KI copies of transplant-file fields plus derived variables. The 2005 study-start restriction is not applied here; it is applied in matching.R.


Adding donor and candidate data
Location: R/add_data/

add_donor_data.R — sets DONOR_ID from the liver record and left-joins donor_deceased; recodes donor HIV NAT, HIV antibody, HCV and hepatitis B core antibody. A liver-only block is inside if (FALSE).
add_candidate_data.R — left-joins cand_kipa on the kidney PX_ID and cand_liin on the liver PX_ID; recodes diabetes, dialysis, BMI, time on dialysis, functional status, and liver candidate yes/no/unknown fields.

Both joins drop duplicated columns with select(-ends_with(".y")) and strip .x suffixes. Neither checks the row count after joining.
add_followup_data.R, add_immuno_data.R, add_malignancy_data.R and add_pra_data.R join other SRTR files into separate objects. main.R does not source them.


Matching
Location: R/matching/matching.R

Restricts tx_slk_final to transplants in 2005 or later and selects the matching and outcome variables as match_df.
Converts the transplant date to a number for the caliper and gives the serology covariates an explicit "Missing" level.
Saves match_df to data-private/.
A commented-out block records the matchit() call that was run in a separate session: logistic propensity score on recipient age, sex and race, last MELD, HCV, primary liver and kidney diagnosis, donor age and sex, HBV surface antigen and CMV; nearest neighbour, ratio 1:5, exact on ERA, 365-day caliper on transplant date.
A disabled block reads the matched result from a file outside the project, joins subclass, weights and distance back to tx_slk_final as matched_df, recodes serologies and sets labels.



Modeling
Location: R/modeling/modeling.R (not sourced; does not parse)
All Cox models use robust standard errors clustered on subclass.

Overall mortality: unadjusted, HIV × era interaction, and within each era
Death-censored kidney and liver graft failure: defines LI_* and KI_* time and event variables, then fits unadjusted, interaction and era-specific models
Proportional hazards checks with cox.zph()
Length of stay among those discharged alive: negative binomial (unadjusted and with era) and log-linear models with cluster-robust standard errors
Era-specific mortality models adjusted for HBV surface antigen and CMV

Models with + ERA (cox_main_effects, cox_kidney_era, cox_liver_era) are commented out, but tables/tables.R uses them.


Tables
Location: R/tables/

Most tables are saved to tables/. One is saved to the project root, and the adjusted-model summary is written to a folder outside the project.


Figures
Location: R/figures/figures.R (main.R sources R/figures.R instead)

Kaplan–Meier survival curves by HIV status, overall and within each era, with risk tables, saved to the project root
Log-rank tests and median survival tables

Data Flow
SRTR files → tx_merged (all liver–kidney record pairs per person) → tx_slkRaw (SLK pairs) → tx_slk_clean (first SLK, no prior transplants, one row per person) → tx_slk_final (HIV classified, exclusions applied, derived, donor and candidate variables added) → match_df (2005 onward, matching variables) → external matchit() run → matched_df (matched cohort with subclass) → models → tables and figures.

Configuration

Data location: sRtr::set_srtr_wd(), called by the person running the analysis before main.R.
Analysis settings are hard-coded where used: one-day SLK window (import.R), age ≥ 16, DAA era cut-off at 2014 and multi-organ exclusions (process_slk_data.R), 2005 study start and matching specification (matching.R).
File outputs: data-private/ (review extracts and match_df), tables/, the project root, and a folder outside the project.

#Functions


#From the combining_liver_kidney_variables.R script
combine_li_ki_consistent <- function(li, ki,
                                     pos_codes = c("Y","P","1"),
                                     neg_codes = c("N","0"),
                                     unknown_codes = c("U","ND","Unknown","", NA),
                                     out_pos = NULL,
                                     out_neg = NULL,
                                     unknown_out = NA_character_,
                                     discordant_out = NA_character_) {
  
  li_chr <- stringr::str_trim(as.character(li))
  ki_chr <- stringr::str_trim(as.character(ki))
  
  # Clean unknowns
  li_clean <- ifelse(li_chr %in% unknown_codes, NA_character_, li_chr)
  ki_clean <- ifelse(ki_chr %in% unknown_codes, NA_character_, ki_chr)
  
  if (is.null(out_pos)) out_pos <- pos_codes[1]
  if (is.null(out_neg)) out_neg <- neg_codes[1]
  
  discordant <- (!is.na(li_clean) & !is.na(ki_clean)) &
    ((li_clean %in% pos_codes & ki_clean %in% neg_codes) |
       (li_clean %in% neg_codes & ki_clean %in% pos_codes))
  
  dplyr::case_when(
    # Explicit P vs N conflict
    discordant ~ discordant_out,
    
    # Positive if P + (P or NA)
    (li_clean %in% pos_codes & (is.na(ki_clean) | ki_clean %in% pos_codes)) ~ out_pos,
    (ki_clean %in% pos_codes & (is.na(li_clean) | li_clean %in% pos_codes)) ~ out_pos,
    
    # Negative if N + N OR N + NA
    (li_clean %in% neg_codes & (is.na(ki_clean) | ki_clean %in% neg_codes)) ~ out_neg,
    (ki_clean %in% neg_codes & (is.na(li_clean) | li_clean %in% neg_codes)) ~ out_neg,
    
    # Everything else
    TRUE ~ unknown_out
  )
}



# --- helper recoders ---
recode_sex_FM <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  dplyr::recode(x,
                "F" = "Female",
                "M" = "Male",
                .default = x
  )
}

recode_YNU_to_words <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  # combine U + Unknown first
  x <- dplyr::recode(x, "Unknown" = "U", .default = x)
  dplyr::recode(x,
                "Y" = "Yes",
                "N" = "No",
                "U" = "Unknown",
                .default = x
  )
}


# SRTR-style donor race codes seen in your table:
collapse_donor_race <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  case_when(
    is.na(x) ~ "Missing",
    x %in% c("8", "White", "WHITE") ~ "White",
    x %in% c("16", "Black or African American", "BLACK") ~ "Black",
    x %in% c("2000", "Hispanic/Latino", "HISPANIC") ~ "Hispanic/Latino",
    # everything else (Asian, AIAN, NHPI, etc.)
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )
}


#Converts a vector of labels into a list object for the gtsummary package
make_gtsummary_labels <- function(named_vec) {
  lapply(names(named_vec), function(v) {
    as.formula(paste0(v, " ~ ", shQuote(unname(named_vec[[v]]))))
  })
}


# Helper: convert NA / "" / " " to "Missing" and return a factor
make_missing_level <- function(x, missing_label = "Missing") {
  x <- as.character(x)
  x <- trimws(x)
  x[x == ""] <- NA
  x[is.na(x)] <- missing_label
  factor(x)
}

# ---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***
# Helper: extract robust HR/CI/p for HIV_POSITIVE
# Uses vcov(fit) -> robust sandwich when you fit with robust=TRUE + cluster=subclass
# ---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***

extract_hiv_row <- function(fit, label, ne = FALSE) {
  if (ne) {
    return(tibble(
      Outcome = label,
      `HR (95% CI)` = "NE",
      p = ""
    ))
  }
  
  term <- "HIV_POSITIVE"
  b <- unname(coef(fit)[term])
  
  # robust SE from vcov (should be robust due to robust=TRUE + cluster=subclass)
  V <- vcov(fit)
  se <- sqrt(unname(V[term, term]))
  
  z  <- b / se
  p  <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))
  
  hr <- exp(b)
  lo <- exp(b - 1.96 * se)
  hi <- exp(b + 1.96 * se)
  
  p_fmt <- ifelse(is.na(p), "",
                  ifelse(p < 0.01, "<0.01", sprintf("%.2f", p)))
  
  tibble(
    Outcome = label,
    `HR (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", hr, lo, hi),
    p = p_fmt
  )
}

# Build the mega results table as a dataframe
# Assumes you already created these Cox fits:
# cox_main, cox_pre_unadj, cox_post_unadj
# cox_kidney, cox_kidney_pre, cox_kidney_post
# cox_liver, cox_liver_pre, cox_liver_post
# ---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***---***

mega_df <- bind_rows(
  # Mortality block (overall/pre/post)
  extract_hiv_row(cox_main,      "Overall mortality — Overall") %>% mutate(ERA = "Overall"),
  extract_hiv_row(cox_pre_unadj, "Overall mortality — Pre-DAA") %>% mutate(ERA = "Pre-DAA"),
  extract_hiv_row(cox_post_unadj,"Overall mortality — Post-DAA")%>% mutate(ERA = "Post-DAA"),
  
  # Kidney graft failure block with event counts in label
  extract_hiv_row(cox_kidney,      "Kidney graft failure (28 events; 6 HIV+) — Overall") %>% mutate(ERA = "Overall"),
  extract_hiv_row(cox_kidney_pre,  "Kidney graft failure (28 events; 6 HIV+) — Pre-DAA") %>% mutate(ERA = "Pre-DAA"),
  extract_hiv_row(cox_kidney_post, "Kidney graft failure (28 events; 6 HIV+) — Post-DAA")%>% mutate(ERA = "Post-DAA"),
  
  # Liver graft failure block with Post-DAA marked NE
  extract_hiv_row(cox_liver,     "Liver graft failure (16 events; 2 HIV+) — Overall") %>% mutate(ERA = "Overall"),
  extract_hiv_row(cox_liver_pre, "Liver graft failure (16 events; 2 HIV+) — Pre-DAA") %>% mutate(ERA = "Pre-DAA"),
  extract_hiv_row(cox_liver_post,"Liver graft failure (16 events; 2 HIV+) — Post-DAA", ne = TRUE) %>% mutate(ERA = "Post-DAA")
) %>%
  # Keep just the outcome group name (without the era suffix) and make a wide table
  mutate(
    OutcomeGroup = sub(" — (Overall|Pre-DAA|Post-DAA)$", "", Outcome)
  ) %>%
  select(OutcomeGroup, ERA, `HR (95% CI)`, p) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = ERA,
    values_from = c(`HR (95% CI)`, p),
    names_glue = "{.value} ({ERA})"
  ) %>%
  rename(Outcome = OutcomeGroup)

library(dplyr)
library(survival)

fmt_p <- function(p) {
  if (is.na(p)) return(NA_character_)
  if (p < 0.01) return("<0.01")
  sprintf("%.2f", p)
}

fmt_hrci <- function(hr, lo, hi) {
  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", hr, lo, hi)
}



extract_interaction <- function(fit, outcome_label,
                                term = "HIV_POSITIVE:ERAPost-DAA") {
  
  # ---- FORCE NE for liver graft failure (sparse post-DAA events) ----
  if (outcome_label == "Liver graft failure (16 events; 2 HIV+)") {
    return(tibble(
      Outcome = outcome_label,
      `Interaction HR (95% CI)` = "NE",
      `Interaction p` = NA_character_
    ))
  }
  
  # ---- If interaction term not present ----
  if (!term %in% names(coef(fit))) {
    return(tibble(
      Outcome = outcome_label,
      `Interaction HR (95% CI)` = NA_character_,
      `Interaction p` = NA_character_
    ))
  }
  
  
  
  b <- unname(coef(fit)[term])
  
  V <- tryCatch(vcov(fit), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(V) || !all(term %in% rownames(V))) {
    return(tibble(
      Outcome = outcome_label,
      `Interaction HR (95% CI)` = NA_character_,
      `Interaction p` = NA_character_
    ))
  }
  
  se <- sqrt(unname(V[term, term]))
  
  # ---- Guard against infinite / zero / NA SE ----
  if (!is.finite(se) || is.na(se) || se <= 0) {
    return(tibble(
      Outcome = outcome_label,
      `Interaction HR (95% CI)` = NA_character_,
      `Interaction p` = NA_character_
    ))
  }
  
  # ---- Compute HR, CI, p ----
  hr <- exp(b)
  lo <- exp(b - 1.96 * se)
  hi <- exp(b + 1.96 * se)
  p  <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(b / se))
  
  tibble(
    Outcome = outcome_label,
    `Interaction HR (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", hr, lo, hi),
    `Interaction p` = ifelse(p < 0.01, "<0.01", sprintf("%.2f", p))
  )
}

#make table for LOS
extract_robust <- function(fit, cluster, model_label,
                           exponentiate = TRUE,
                           keep_terms = NULL) {
  
  ct <- coeftest(fit, vcov = vcovCL(fit, cluster = cluster))
  
  df <- tibble(
    Model    = model_label,
    term     = rownames(ct),
    estimate = as.numeric(ct[, 1]),
    se       = as.numeric(ct[, 2]),
    p.value  = as.numeric(ct[, ncol(ct)])
  )
  
  if (!is.null(keep_terms)) df <- df %>% dplyr::filter(term %in% keep_terms)
  
  df <- df %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      conf.low  = estimate - 1.96 * se,
      conf.high = estimate + 1.96 * se
    )
  
  if (exponentiate) {
    df <- df %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        est = exp(estimate),
        lo  = exp(conf.low),
        hi  = exp(conf.high),
        pct = (est - 1) * 100
      )
  } else {
    df <- df %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        est = estimate,
        lo  = conf.low,
        hi  = conf.high,
        pct = NA_real_
      )
  }
  
  df %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      Predictor = dplyr::case_when(
        term == "HIV_POSITIVE" ~ "HIV-positive (vs HIV-negative)",
        term == "ERAPost-DAA"  ~ "Post-DAA era (vs Pre-DAA)",
        term == "(Intercept)" ~ "Intercept",
        TRUE ~ term
      ),
      `Effect (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", est, lo, hi),
      `Approx. % diff`  = ifelse(is.na(pct), NA_character_, sprintf("%+.1f%%", pct)),
      `p-value` = dplyr::case_when(
        is.na(p.value) ~ NA_character_,
        p.value < 0.001 ~ "<0.001",
        TRUE ~ sprintf("%.3f", p.value)
      )
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(Model, Predictor, `Effect (95% CI)`, `Approx. % diff`, `p-value`)
}


# --- helper: format one cox model nicely ---

format_cox <- function(fit, model_name = "Model") {
  s <- summary(fit)
  n <- s$n
  events <- s$nevent
  
  # broom table (robust SEs are already baked into coef(summary(fit)) when robust=TRUE)
  out <- broom::tidy(fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
    mutate(
      model = model_name,
      n = n,
      events = events,
      # nicer labels
      term = case_when(
        term == "HIV_POSITIVE" ~ "HIV positive (vs negative)",
        term == "ERAPost-DAA" ~ "Post-DAA (vs Pre-DAA)",
        term == "HIV_POSITIVE:ERAPost-DAA" ~ "Interaction: HIV × Post-DAA",
        str_detect(term, "^REC_HBV_SURF_ANTIGEN_COMB") ~ str_replace(term, "^REC_HBV_SURF_ANTIGEN_COMB", "HBsAg: "),
        str_detect(term, "^REC_CMV_COMBINED") ~ str_replace(term, "^REC_CMV_COMBINED", "CMV: "),
        TRUE ~ term
      ),
      hr_ci = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f)", estimate, conf.low, conf.high),
      p_fmt = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))
    ) %>%
    select(model, n, events, term, hr_ci, p_fmt)
  
  out
}

# --- helper: capture warnings while fitting (optional) ---
fit_cox_capture_warning <- function(expr) {
  w <- NULL
  fit <- withCallingHandlers(
    expr,
    warning = function(m) {
      w <<- c(w, conditionMessage(m))
      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
    }
  )
  list(fit = fit, warnings = w)
}

The project
This repository compares mortality and graft outcomes after simultaneous liver–kidney (SLK) transplantation between recipients with and without HIV. It uses Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR) standard analysis files, and it publishes its code and methods as a Quarto website.

analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. It covers the cohort, exposure, era, matching, outcomes, models, and sensitivity analyses. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it.

The plan contains no code: no scripts, functions, objects, packages beyond those named as methods, or descriptions of what the code currently does. Rules for the code go in this file, a description of the code in ARCHITECTURE.md, and gaps between the code and the plan in Issues. SRTR variable names are data definitions and may appear in the plan.
Plan changes are tracked in git, not in a change log inside the plan. Commit each design change on its own, with a message that gives the reason and says whether any results that depend on it had already been seen.

Open decisions. The plan marks each open design choice Open: where it occurs, linked to its decision issue (titled “Decision Dn”). Do not settle one in code. Until it is settled, the code keeps the behaviour that produced the poster results and says so in a comment that names the decision. If the code needs to depart from the plan, open a decision issue, or comment on the existing one. Once the decider has settled it (in the issue, or relayed there in his exact words), the plan change and the code can go in the same pull request, which closes the issue.
Decider. Scientific decisions are made by Vagish Hemmige. Anyone may open or contribute to a decision issue; only the decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
This is an analysis project, not an R package, even though the scripts live in R/ and there is an .Rbuildignore. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or pkgdown infrastructure. Do not apply CRAN conventions.
Default branch: master, protected. Changes reach it only through pull requests.
Implementation status lives in GitHub Issues, not in these files. When you find a gap between the code and the plan, or a defect, open or update an issue. Reference the issue in the pull request that closes it.

Record the sRtr version (or commit) used for any result.

Exploration and definitive analysis
Exploration is welcome on branches, or in R/exploratory/, which main.R never sources. Exploratory scripts need not have Quarto pages, and their findings are labelled preliminary. Exploration code does not stay in pipeline scripts. A script becomes part of the definitive analysis when it is sourced from R/main.R; from then on every rule below applies to it.

R scripts

Running the analysis. Open the .Rproj and run R/main.R from the project root. main.R sources the other scripts in dependency order; ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each does.
One job per script. Scripts are grouped by stage: R/primary_data_preparation/ (import and cohort construction), R/add_data/ (merging candidate and donor files), R/matching/, R/modeling/, then R/tables.R and R/figures.R. When you add a definitive script, in the same pull request:

source it from main.R (or from tables.R or figures.R) at the right point
add its Quarto page
update ARCHITECTURE.md

Header comment. Each script begins with a comment saying what it does, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, and what it produces.
Constants, libraries, and code lists live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code values. Any number a reader might want to change, such as the study start year, the era cut-off, the age threshold, the matching ratio, the caliper, or the seed, is a named constant in setup.R.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R, sourced after setup.R. functions.R defines functions only; it never runs analysis code. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects, including through default arguments.
No side effects outside the project. Do not use setwd(), absolute paths, ~/ paths, or writes outside the project. Locate data only through sRtr::set_srtr_wd(), called by the person running the analysis, not in committed code.
No results in the repository. No script (exploratory or definitive), comment, commit message, issue, pull-request text or review report contains results, counts or data values from SRTR data unless they are cleared for release. Check before every commit and post, since this public repository publishes everything pushed to it, on any branch.
Legacy code. rmd/SLK_1.8.rmd and rmd/SLK_2.8.rmd are the R Markdown notebooks the pipeline was split from. They are not run and are kept for reference only. Do not build on them.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections, so that Quarto pages can show the code without copying it:
## ---- exclude-prior-transplants

Every logical step has a label. A label covers the code from its line to the next label.
Labels are kebab-case, describe the step, and are unique across all scripts. Quarto pulls chunks by label, so a duplicate label silently picks up the wrong code.
Renaming or deleting a label breaks the Quarto page that uses it. Search the .qmd files before you change one.
Scripts must still run end to end through main.R. Labels are comments and must never change what the code does.

Variable labels

Label analysis variables with human-readable descriptions, for example with labelled::set_variable_labels(). Tables then show readable names without renaming code by hand.
For SRTR variables, load files with load_srtr_file(..., factor_labels = TRUE, var_labels = TRUE) and use apply_srtr_varlabels() and apply_srtr_factors() rather than writing labels by hand.
Label each derived variable where it is created. Include units and the source fields where they apply (for example, “Time to death or censoring from composite transplant date, years”).

Quarto website
The Quarto site documents the code. It does not run the analysis.

Setup files: _quarto.yml, index.qmd, 404.qmd (the page GitHub Pages shows for a missing address) and styles.css sit at the root. There is one page per pipeline script in quarto/, named after the script (for example, quarto/process_slk_data.qmd for R/primary_data_preparation/process_slk_data.R), plus the project-document and About pages. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode, Results and Pending callouts.
Visual cues. Each kind of page has one sidebar icon, coloured by styles.css, and pages mark the same kind of content with the callout of that colour: background book (blue); study design and methods diagram-3 (orange); R code laptop (pink, Rcode 💻); results clipboard-data (green, Results 📊); project documents file-earmark-ruled (grey). Give every new page the icon of its kind.
Provisional content. quarto/_pending.lua highlights in yellow every paragraph that starts with Decision pending: or, in the plan, Open:, and any [text]{.pending}, and adds a ⏳ Pending callout to pages that have a mark. Mark only what an open decision could change, and remove the mark when the decision is settled.
Project documents. analysis-plan.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md and REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md are shown on the site by pages in quarto/ that only include the root file, which stays the one source: edit the root file, not the page.
Showing code: each page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk() in a hidden chunk. It then shows each labelled section in a chunk with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why. Until a script is divided into labelled sections, its page may show the whole script with #| file: and eval: false. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. Pages must render without SRTR data. _quarto.yml sets eval: false for every chunk; only the read_chunk() imports, the Setup page’s chunks that attach packages and build its package table from text, and the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md set eval: true. The rendered site therefore contains code and explanation only, never results. The one exception is the poster on the home page, which was already approved for public release.
Rendering: the site renders to docs/, which is not committed. .github/workflows/publish.yml renders it on every pull request as a check and, on each push to master, publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. Render locally to preview a change to a script’s labels or a page’s prose, but do not commit the output.
New scripts: when you add a script, add its page and its sidebar entry in _quarto.yml in the same pull request.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update that section’s explanation in the same pull request.

Outputs

Exported files: tables and figures are exported by R/tables.R and R/figures.R to tables/ and figures/. Both folders are gitignored until they are cleared for release under the disclosure rules below, because their contents are results from SRTR data. Agents may not open them (see Restricted data).
Intermediate files that must be written (for example, records exported for manual review) go in data-private/, which is gitignored. The pipeline must not depend on a file someone edited by hand; encode the decision made from a manual review as a reproducible rule in code, with a comment explaining it.
Figures need alt text when they are published.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md. Edit the .Rmd and re-knit; do not edit README.md directly.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)
The Access column of “Data sources” says which sources are restricted. SRTR data are covered by the SRTR data use agreement (DUA). The rules below apply to people and agents alike.

Never commit data. That includes SRTR files, extracts, and any saved R object or output derived from patient-level data (.rds, .RData, .sas7bdat, .parquet, .csv, .xlsx, and the like). Keep data outside the repository, and check .gitignore before adding a new output type.
No patient-level values in code or comments. Do not write identifiers (PERS_ID, PX_ID, TRR_ID, DONOR_ID), dates, or counts from the data into scripts or comments. Code must not print identifiers or rows of patient-level data; checks use stopifnot() or stop() rather than printing.
AI agents never read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents therefore do not:

open data files or patient-level objects
print rows or head() of them
display identifiers, person-level dates, or individual records
open outputs from SRTR data that are not yet cleared for release (for example tables/ and figures/ while they are gitignored)

Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data that mimics the column names and types. Results on real data are produced by an authorized person. The only exception is what the “Data sources” table explicitly allows for a source, and only within those words.
Use synthetic data for development and tests. Build small synthetic data frames in code, label them clearly as synthetic, and never derive them from real records.
Disclosure. Check every table, figure, flowchart box, risk table, and piece of text before it leaves the secure environment, against the exact wording of the SRTR DUA. This includes scripts, comments, commit messages, issues, pull-request text and review reports. The small-cell rule is open decision D8 in the plan; until it is settled, ask the maintainer before releasing any count below 11. Figures that plot individual people are not published.
Credentials and paid APIs. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron. Ask before paid, bulk, or uncached API calls. Which model or service version to use is the person’s choice; an agent proposes, with the cost if known, and does not switch it on its own.

Coding conventions

Flowchart labels and text are built from the constants in setup.R, not hard-coded. For example, a label that says “2005 or later” or “age 16 or older” goes stale when the constants change.
Cohort flow uses the flowchart package (as_fc(), fc_filter(), fc_draw()). Every exclusion goes through fc_filter(), in the plan’s order. Never drop rows from $data outside the flowchart; the diagram must reproduce the cohort exactly. Record-level processing (harmonizing liver and kidney copies, choosing among a person’s records) is fine. An analysis that uses fewer people than the cohort (complete cases, a subgroup) reports its own number with that analysis. The cohort used downstream is the data from the final flowchart step.
Matching

Matching runs inside the pipeline and is reproducible from the seed in setup.R. Control selection must not depend on row order.
The matched-set identifier (subclass) is kept as an ordinary column through to every model, so models can cluster on it.
Report the number of HIV-positive recipients with each number of matched controls, including zero, and balance (standardized mean differences) before and after matching.

Joins

Use join_by() with an explicit relationship where you can.
After every join of a supplementary file (candidate, donor, follow-up) to the cohort, assert that it did not multiply rows.
Decide deliberately what happens to people with no match: keep them, exclude them through a flowchart step, or stop with an error.
Avoid select(-ends_with(".y")) after a join; it silently keeps one copy of a duplicated column. Select the columns you need from the supplementary file before joining.

Code lists (diagnosis or organ codes, for example) carry each code’s meaning and the dictionary release it was checked against. Check every code against the SRTR data dictionary. Never invent codes, variables, files, or definitions.
Dates and times

Compute times from Date columns with difftime(..., units = "days"), and state the conversion to years (365.25 days).
Death-censored outcomes end at the earliest of event, death, and last follow-up; test the edges on synthetic data.

Models. Keep code that formats model results (hazard ratios, intervals, p-values) in named functions in R/functions.R, and test them on synthetic data with a known answer. Table labels such as event counts are computed from the data, never typed in.
Package APIs. Read the help page and NEWS for the installed version before calling a package; don’t write calls from memory. A test that fakes a package checks only our own logic, so call the real package once (on synthetic data) before relying on the code.
Style: readable for a clinician-analyst who learned R from online guides: pipes and dplyr/tidyr verbs, case_when() rather than nested if, and loops over names or named lists rather than the apply family, Reduce() or positional indexing. Where base R is required, keep it in a named, tested function with a comment saying why. Follow the tidyverse style guide. Style changes go in their own commits, separate from changes that alter analytical behaviour.

Checks for any change
Before opening a pull request, check the items below that apply to your change.
Plan and data sources

Does the change implement the plan as written, and does it leave every open decision open?
Does it use sRtr’s functions where they exist, and does their documented behaviour match what the plan needs?
For new or changed calls to a package, does the pull request name the installed version and the help page or NEWS entry relied on?

Cohort construction

Do the order, the denominator, and the labels of each flowchart step match the condition it applies?
Can each count be reproduced from the code?
Is the downstream cohort the data from the final flowchart step?
Is there exactly one row per PERS_ID after the duplicate steps?

Exposure, era and covariates

Is HIV status classified as the plan states (Section 5.1, D2)?
Are liver and kidney copies of each covariate harmonized by a documented rule?
Is every covariate measured at or before transplant?

Matching

Does the propensity score model contain exactly the covariates in the plan (Section 6.2, D3)?
Are era exact matching, the transplant-date caliper, and the ratio taken from setup.R?
Is matching reproducible from the seed, and independent of row order?
Are unmatched and partially matched HIV-positive recipients counted and reported?

Outcomes

Does follow-up for mortality start at the composite transplant date and end at death or the latest last follow-up date?
Are graft failure outcomes death-censored, starting at that organ’s transplant date?
Are recipients who died before discharge excluded from length of stay?

Models and reported numbers

Does every Cox model use robust standard errors clustered on subclass?
Does each estimate match the plan’s estimand, and do the tables, figures, and website prose say what the model actually estimates?
Are event counts and sample sizes in labels computed, not typed?

Structure and documentation

Is ARCHITECTURE.md current for the scripts and data flow this change touches?
Are the chunk labels unique, and does each script’s Quarto page still find every label it uses?
Does every pipeline script have a Quarto page and a sidebar entry, and does the pull request’s render check pass?
Does any site chunk run analysis code? Only the chunks listed under “Quarto website” set eval: true.
Are new derived variables labelled?

Disclosure

Search every changed tracked file, and the commit messages and pull-request text, for dates, record IDs, names, absolute paths and numbers that could come from SRTR data. Read each hit in context; legitimate ones (plan dates, the decider’s name, synthetic examples) stay.

Execution

Does main.R run from a clean session (Ctrl+Shift+F10 in RStudio, then source main.R), with no objects left over from earlier work?
Are paths relative, with no hard-coded data directories?
Are package versions recorded (sessionInfo(), and the sRtr commit)?

Validation on real data (run by an authorized person; report only aggregate, disclosure-checked results)

counts at each flowchart step, compared with the poster and manuscript
row counts before and after each join of a supplementary file
the number of HIV-positive recipients with 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0 matched controls
standardized mean differences before and after matching
events by group for each outcome, overall and by era

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent sets its working style (review only, step by step, or hands-off) in their own instructions, and may add stricter rules; those take precedence over this section. Without a style, an agent works step by step. At most, an agent may:

edit code and documentation
add scripts and tests
run code and render the site on synthetic data
commit to a branch and open a pull request

Collaborators: master is protected. Changes reach it only through a pull request that the maintainer reviews.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to a decision issue. The decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any level of autonomy:

never merges a pull request
follows the restricted-data rules above
asks before any step that would read real data, run the full pipeline, or make expensive calls
shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this
proposes another way of writing something already agreed before committing it

Keep pull requests focused. In each one, state which section of the plan or which issue it addresses, and what was checked. Say whether it was checked on synthetic data or by reading only. Never describe synthetic results as results.
For references, use the SRTR data dictionary and documentation, and PubMed. Cite what you used, and verify every citation (authors, journal, year, DOI) against PubMed before adding it to references.bib.

1. Objective
To compare all-cause mortality after simultaneous liver–kidney (SLK) transplantation between recipients with HIV and propensity-score-matched recipients without HIV, in the United States, 2005–2023.
Secondary objectives

Compare death-censored kidney graft failure and death-censored liver graft failure.
Compare post-transplant hospital length of stay among recipients discharged alive.
Assess whether the association between HIV and each outcome differs between the eras before and after direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) for hepatitis C.

Planned future aim (not part of this analysis): compare SLK recipients with HIV to liver-only recipients with HIV.

Open: D9 (#19): whether this comparison is part of this paper or a separate analysis.

2. Design
Retrospective matched cohort study in national transplant registry data. Each HIV-positive SLK recipient is matched to up to five HIV-negative SLK recipients on a propensity score, with exact matching on DAA era and a caliper on transplant date (Section 6). All outcome analyses are conducted in the matched cohort.
The draft manuscript calls the design a “matched case-control study”. Because exposure (HIV) defines the groups and outcomes are followed forward from transplant, this plan describes it as a matched cohort.

3. Data source

Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR) standard analysis files, Spring 2023 release, accessed under a data use agreement.

Transplant recipient files: liver (tx_li) and kidney (tx_ki).
Candidate files: kidney–pancreas (cand_kipa) and liver/intestine (cand_liin).
Deceased donor file (donor_deceased).
Follow-up files (txf_li, txf_ki) where a variable requires them.

Linkage: liver and kidney transplant records are linked within SRTR by the person identifier PERS_ID. Candidate records are linked by PX_ID, and donor records by DONOR_ID. No external linkage is performed.
Period: transplants in the release run from 1987-01-01 to 2023-03-31. The study period is 2005-01-01 to 2023-03-31, because the first SLK transplant in a recipient with HIV in the data occurred in 2005.
Ethics: approved by the Albert Einstein College of Medicine Institutional Review Board (IRB #2021-13273); de-identified data.

4. Study population

4.1 SLK definition
An SLK transplant is a liver transplant and a kidney transplant in the same person (PERS_ID) on the same day, plus or minus one day.


4.2 Inclusion

SLK transplant during the study period (Section 3).
Recipient age at transplant of at least 16 years (see D1 below).
Non-missing identifiers needed for linkage and follow-up, including the donor identifier in both files.


Open: D1 (#11): the age threshold (the poster cohort used ≥16 years; the manuscript says “greater than 16” and “adult”).



4.3 Exclusion

Any prior transplant of any organ, identified both from the prior-transplant fields (CAN_PREV_TX) and from an earlier transplant date in either file.
Additional organs at the SLK transplant (kidney–liver–heart, kidney–liver–intestine).
Liver and kidney allografts from different donors.
HIV status recorded as positive in one file and negative in the other (Section 5.1).

If a recipient has more than one SLK transplant, only the first is used. Same-day duplicate records are resolved to one record per recipient by a documented, reproducible rule.

5. Exposure, era, and time zero

5.1 Exposure definition
Recipient HIV serostatus at transplant, from REC_HIV_STAT in the liver and kidney files.

HIV-positive: positive in at least one file, and positive or missing/unknown in the other.
HIV-negative: every other non-discordant recipient, including those whose status is unknown or not done in both files.
Discordant (positive in one file, negative in the other): excluded (Section 4.3).


Open: D2 (#12): the manuscript says a positive status must be “not contradicted by an ‘unknown’ designation” in the other file, while the poster cohort classified positive-plus-unknown as positive. Because HIV-negative includes unknown status, tables label that group “Negative/Unknown”.



5.2 DAA era

Pre-DAA: transplant year 2005–2013.
Post-DAA: transplant year 2014–2023.

2014 is the first year in which DAA therapy was widely available to transplant recipients.


5.3 Time zero
The composite transplant date: the earlier of the liver and kidney transplant dates. For organ-specific graft outcomes, time zero is that organ’s transplant date. Covariates are measured at or before transplant.

6. Matching

6.1 Method

Propensity score: probability of HIV-positive status, estimated by logistic regression.
Exact matching on DAA era.
Caliper of 365 days on the transplant date.
Nearest-neighbour matching without replacement, ratio 1:5 (up to five HIV-negative recipients per HIV-positive recipient).
No caliper on the propensity score itself.
Matching is reproducible, and the matched set is carried through to every outcome model.

6.3 Matching outcomes reported

The number of HIV-positive recipients with 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0 matched controls.
HIV-positive recipients excluded or unmatched, and how they compare with those matched.
The proportion of matched sets in which members differ by more than the caliper, as a check.

7. Outcomes

7.1 Primary outcome: all-cause mortality

Death date: a composite of registry sources, in order of priority: OPTN-reported death date (PERS_OPTN_DEATH_DT), Social Security Administration death date (PERS_SSA_DEATH_DT), then transplant follow-up death date (TFL_DEATH_DT), taking whichever file (liver or kidney) records it.
Censoring: recipients without a death date are censored at the latest last-follow-up date (TFL_LAFUDATE) across the liver and kidney files.
Time: from the composite transplant date to death or censoring, in years.



7.2 Secondary outcomes: death-censored graft failure
Evaluated separately for the kidney and the liver graft.

Event: registry-reported graft failure date (TFL_GRAFT_DT) for that organ.
Follow-up ends at the earliest of graft failure, death, or that organ’s last follow-up date. Death before graft failure is censored.
Time: from that organ’s transplant date, in years.


Open: D5 (#15): whether retransplantation of the organ (PERS_NEXTTX) or return to chronic dialysis without a recorded graft failure date also counts as graft failure.



7.3 Secondary outcome: hospital length of stay

Days from transplant date to transplant discharge date (REC_DISCHRG_DT), counted inclusively so that the transplant day is day 1.
Recipients who died on or before the recorded discharge date are excluded from this analysis.

8. Statistical analysis

8.1 Descriptive analysis

A cohort flow diagram from all SLK transplants in the release through each exclusion to the matched cohort.
Baseline donor and recipient characteristics by HIV status, before and after matching: median and interquartile range for continuous variables, counts and percentages for categorical variables.
Unadjusted comparisons: Wilcoxon rank-sum test for continuous variables, and chi-square or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, as appropriate.



8.2 Balance

Standardized mean differences for every propensity score covariate, before and after matching.
An absolute standardized mean difference below 0.10 is considered adequate balance.
Balance is assessed before any outcome analysis is run.



8.3 Survival analysis

Kaplan–Meier estimates of patient survival by HIV status, compared with the log-rank test; overall and within each DAA era.
Cox proportional hazards models for HIV status and each time-to-event outcome (mortality, kidney graft failure, liver graft failure), with robust standard errors clustered on matched set.
The proportional hazards assumption is checked with scaled Schoenfeld residuals.



8.4 Effect modification by DAA era

Cox models fitted separately within the pre-DAA and post-DAA matched cohorts. Matched sets stay within one era because era is matched exactly.
A model with an HIV × era interaction in the full matched cohort, to test for effect modification. The interaction hazard ratio is the ratio of the post-DAA to the pre-DAA hazard ratio.


Open: D7 (#17): whether era-specific models are reported unadjusted only (as on the poster), or also with adjustment for covariates with residual imbalance after matching (for example, HBV surface antigen and CMV).


Open: D10 (#20): handling of sparse or zero events (for example, liver graft failure in the post-DAA era): report as not estimable, or use Firth’s penalized Cox regression.



8.5 Length of stay
Compared between groups with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, because of its right-skewed distribution.

Open: D6 (#16): whether length of stay is also analysed by regression (negative binomial or log-linear, with standard errors clustered on matched set) as a secondary analysis.



8.6 Missing data

Missingness of every covariate and outcome field is described by HIV status.
Missing categorical covariates are an explicit category (Section 6.2); continuous covariates follow D4.



8.7 Inference and software

All tests are two-sided, with p < 0.05 considered statistically significant.
Analyses are run in R (version 4.5.1 for the poster results), with propensity score matching in MatchIt.
Code is public at https://github.com/VagishHemmige/HIV-SLK-outcomes, and a website at https://vagishhemmige.github.io/HIV-SLK-outcomes documents each step. Data are not shared, as the data use agreement requires.

9. Sensitivity analyses

HCV-positive recipients: the matched cohort restricted to recipients with HCV-positive serostatus, with the primary Cox model and era-specific models, to assess whether the association differs among those directly affected by DAAs.
Missing-data handling: the alternative under D4 to the one chosen as primary.
Exposure classification: the alternative rule under D2 for positive-plus-unknown recipients.

10. Disclosure control

All outputs are reviewed against the SRTR data use agreement before they leave the secure environment.
Figures that show individual people are not published.


Open: D8 (#18): the small-cell rule for tables, figures, flow diagrams, risk tables and website text, under the exact wording of the SRTR data use agreement (for example, suppressing counts below 11).

11. Limitations to address in reporting

Small number of HIV-positive SLK recipients, limiting power, especially for graft failure and era-specific analyses.
HIV status from registry fields, with unknown status grouped with HIV-negative; some misclassification is possible.
No HIV-specific clinical data (CD4 count, viral load, antiretroviral regimen) in the standard analysis files.
Residual confounding by unmeasured factors, including center practices.
Registry follow-up and graft failure ascertainment vary by center and over time.
